item.title: Curious, but Clever: Uncertainty-Directed Exploration and Preference Gradient Bandits
item.dc:creator: Varun Ravi Varma
item.description:
NoteIn brief

In the preceding episode, we established how sample-average updates and -greedy action selection navigate the tension between empirical exploitation and stochastic exploration. Nonetheless, selecting actions uniformly at random during exploratory intervals incurs linear regret because the agent samples known inferior actions with equal likelihood. This episode formalises uncertainty-directed exploration and preference-based gradient learning. Specifically, we delineate optimistic initialisation, derive the Upper Confidence Bound (UCB1) algorithm to achieve logarithmic regret, substantiate soft-max policy gradient updates via stochastic gradient ascent, and introduce associative search as the conceptual bridge toward full Markov Decision Processes (Sutton and Barto 2018; Auer et al. 2002; Lai and Robbins 1985).

0.1 Episode Metadata

  • Game: Candy machines with a twist
  • Source: Sutton & Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (2nd ed.), Chapter 2, §2.6–2.10 (Sutton and Barto 2018)
  • Series Index: RL from First Principles
  • Story
  • Idea
  • Maths & Code

The following weekend, Ada and Grandpa Leo return to the autumn fairground. The candy booth has expanded substantially: an extended row of colourful vintage dispensers now stretches across the pavilion.

“Too many to check one by one with a handful of tokens,” Ada observes, surveying the line with dismay.

Grandpa Leo retrieves a piece of chalk and draws a conspicuous question mark over each dispenser that Ada has barely touched. “A dispenser you know very little about might harbour an extraordinary payout,” he notes with a smile. “To discover its potential, we must provide those unfamiliar levers with a fair appraisal.”

Ada conceives a methodical heuristic. She begins her trial by pretending every single dispenser is exceptionally generous, recording an initial tally of ten sweets beside every machine on her napkin. Each time a machine dispenses merely one or two sweets, the disappointing outcome pulls its running average downwards. Consequently, this initial optimism compels her to test every machine at least once or twice before settling upon an apparent favourite.

Furthermore, Ada refines her exploratory strategy. Instead of pulling levers entirely at random when curious, she prioritises the dispensers enveloped by the greatest uncertainty. A dispenser pulled forty times has yielded its secrets; its empirical performance is corroborated with high confidence. Conversely, a dispenser pulled only once remains an enigma whose true distribution might easily eclipse the current front-runner.

“Curious,” Grandpa Leo observes, admiring her napkin, “yet genuinely clever in where you direct that curiosity.”

By late afternoon, the booth keeper introduces a final twist. Each dispenser is equipped with an overhead indicator lamp that alternates between red and blue. When the illumination is red, the dispensers on the left flank prove consistently superior; when blue, the rightmost bank yields the greatest bounty.

Ada ceases asking “Which dispenser is universally superior?” Instead, she conditions her decision upon the immediate context: “Which dispenser manifests the highest payout when the lamp glows this colour?” Within moments, she glances at the context lamp and navigates directly to the optimal machine.

TipWhat Would You Do?

Is it more advantageous to explore options entirely at random, or to deliberately allocate exploratory trials to the options about which you possess the least empirical evidence?

0.2 Moving Beyond Undirected Exploration

While an -greedy policy guarantees asymptotic convergence to true action values by perturbing decisions uniformly with probability , its exploratory mechanism is fundamentally undirected. The agent expends valuable trials pulling alternatives regardless of whether an alternative has been tested a thousand times or never touched.

To mitigate this inefficiency, we employ two distinct paradigms:

  1. Optimism in the Face of Uncertainty: By instilling an initial prior belief that all actions yield maximal reward (), the agent is systematically driven by empirical disappointment to sample every untried action during early iterations.
  2. Confidence-Directed Selection (UCB): By augmenting each value estimate with an uncertainty bonus proportional to , action selection leverages the upper bound of a statistical confidence interval. An action is selected either because its empirical payoff estimate is superior or because its estimate remains heavily unverified.

0.3 What to Notice

  • Optimism Fades Naturally: Optimistic initial values drive heavy exploration early on, but the drive is temporary: once the estimates fall to realistic levels it vanishes, so optimism alone cannot track machines whose payouts drift.
  • Logarithmic Regret: Under UCB1, the expected number of pulls of any suboptimal action grows only as , so its contribution to regret is , in contrast to the linear regret incurred by constant -greedy policies.
  • Preferences vs Absolute Values: Gradient bandits do not estimate expected returns directly; instead, they optimise a relative preference manifold invariant to global reward translation when an empirical baseline is subtracted.

0.4 Try It: Four Ways to Explore

All four strategies on the 10-armed testbed, simulated live in your browser and averaged over many independent problems. Defaults follow Sutton & Barto: optimistic greedy uses , and (Figure 2.3), UCB uses (Figure 2.4). Shift every true value up by and untick the baseline to reproduce Figure 2.5; switch on drift to watch optimism fade.

import {makeRng, argmaxRandom, runTestbed, toRows, observeTheme, palette} from "../../assets/ojs/rl.js"
theme = Generators.observe(observeTheme)
pal = palette(theme)
viewof explore = Inputs.form({
  runs: Inputs.range([50, 1000], {step: 50, value: 200, label: "Problems averaged"}),
  epsilon: Inputs.range([0, 0.3], {step: 0.01, value: 0.1, label: "ε (ε-greedy)"}),
  q0: Inputs.range([0, 10], {step: 0.5, value: 5, label: "Q₁ (optimistic)"}),
  c: Inputs.range([0, 4], {step: 0.1, value: 2, label: "c (UCB)"}),
  alpha: Inputs.range([0.01, 0.5], {step: 0.01, value: 0.1, label: "α (gradient)"}),
  baseline: Inputs.toggle({label: "Gradient baseline", value: true}),
  shift: Inputs.toggle({label: "Shift q* by +4", value: false}),
  drift: Inputs.toggle({label: "Drifting machines", value: false})
})
exploreNames = ["ε-greedy", "Optimistic greedy", "UCB", "Gradient bandit"]
exploreRows = {
  const common = {
    runs: explore.runs, steps: explore.drift ? 3000 : 1000, seed: 7,
    nonstationary: explore.drift, offset: explore.shift ? 4 : 0
  };
  const series = [
    {name: exploreNames[0], ...runTestbed({...common, epsilon: explore.epsilon})},
    {name: exploreNames[1], ...runTestbed({...common, epsilon: 0, alpha: 0.1, q0: explore.q0 + common.offset})},
    {name: exploreNames[2], ...runTestbed({...common, method: "ucb", c: explore.c})},
    {name: exploreNames[3], ...runTestbed({...common, method: "gradient", alpha: explore.alpha, baseline: explore.baseline})}
  ];
  return toRows(series, common.steps / 200);
}
explorePlot = (y, label, domain) => Plot.plot({
  width: Math.min(width, 760),
  height: 250,
  marginLeft: 50,
  style: {background: "transparent"},
  x: {label: "Step"},
  y: {label, grid: true, domain},
  color: {domain: exploreNames, range: [pal.orange, pal.magenta, pal.blue, pal.green], legend: true},
  marks: [Plot.lineY(exploreRows, {x: "step", y, stroke: "series", strokeWidth: 1.5})]
})
explorePlot("optimal", "% optimal action", [0, 100])
explorePlot("reward", "Average reward", undefined)

The optimistic start is set relative to the shifted values, so Q₁ always means “this far above the average arm”.

WarningCommon Misconception

Misconception: “Exploratory steps are wasted reward.” Reality: An exploratory pull costs reward now but buys information: it narrows the uncertainty about an action, and that knowledge pays off on every later decision. Over a long horizon, directed exploration such as UCB gives up far less reward than either never exploring or exploring at random.

0.5 Optimistic Initial Values (§2.6)

Let the initial action-value estimates be set to an optimistic bound:

Under a standard greedy selection policy , the estimates are updated with a constant step size :

The constant step size matters. Under sample-averaging, the first update uses step size , so and the optimistic prior is erased after a single pull: optimism then only guarantees that every action is tried once. With constant , the prior decays geometrically as , so it keeps influencing selection for several pulls of each action (Sutton & Barto use and in Figure 2.3).

Because greatly exceeds every , early rewards satisfy with high probability (not almost surely: Gaussian rewards are unbounded), so the error term is typically negative. Consequently, each selected action suffers empirical degradation, driving the greedy argmax to cycle through the less-tried actions. Nonetheless, this mechanism is ill-suited for non-stationary environments where drifting distributions require persistent, recurring exploration.

0.6 Upper-Confidence-Bound Selection (§2.7)

The Upper Confidence Bound (UCB1) formalism chooses action according to:

where denotes the total number of elapsed steps, is the cumulative count of arm selections prior to step , and governs exploration intensity. If , action is deemed a maximising action a priori.

0.6.1 Try It: Watching the Confidence Bonus Shrink

Step UCB through a five-armed problem one pull at a time. Each dot is the estimate ; the bar above it is the bonus , and the highlighted arm is the one with the highest upper bound, which UCB pulls next.

viewof ucbC = Inputs.range([0, 4], {step: 0.1, value: 2, label: "c"})
ucbState = {
  const k = 5;
  const s = {k, reveal: false};
  s.reset = () => {
    s.rng = makeRng(Math.floor(Math.random() * 1e9));
    s.q = Array.from({length: k}, () => s.rng.normal(0, 1));
    s.Q = new Array(k).fill(0);
    s.N = new Array(k).fill(0);
    s.t = 0;
    s.last = null;
  };
  s.upper = (c) => s.Q.map((Q, a) => s.N[a] === 0 ? Infinity : Q + c * Math.sqrt(Math.log(s.t + 1) / s.N[a]));
  s.step = (c) => {
    const a = argmaxRandom(s.upper(c), s.rng);
    const R = s.rng.normal(s.q[a], 1);
    s.N[a] += 1;
    s.Q[a] += (R - s.Q[a]) / s.N[a];
    s.t += 1;
    s.last = {a, R};
  };
  s.reset();
  return s;
}
ucbStepper = {
  const s = ucbState;
  const root = html`<div>
    <div class="rl-chart"></div>
    <div class="rl-stats"></div>
    <div>
      <button data-n="1">Pull once</button>
      <button data-n="10">Pull 10×</button>
      <button data-n="100">Pull 100×</button>
      <button data-act="reveal">Reveal q*</button>
      <button data-act="reset">New problem</button>
    </div>
  </div>`;
  const render = () => {
    const upper = s.upper(ucbC);
    const next = upper.indexOf(Math.max(...upper));
    const data = s.Q.map((Q, a) => ({
      arm: `Arm ${a + 1}`, Q, N: s.N[a], q: s.q[a],
      hi: Number.isFinite(upper[a]) ? upper[a] : null, next: a === next
    }));
    const finite = data.filter((d) => d.hi !== null);
    const top = Math.max(3, ...finite.map((d) => d.hi));
    root.querySelector(".rl-chart").replaceChildren(Plot.plot({
      width: Math.min(width, 640),
      height: 260,
      marginLeft: 45,
      style: {background: "transparent"},
      x: {label: null, padding: 0.4},
      y: {label: "Value", grid: true, domain: [-3, top]},
      marks: [
        Plot.barY(finite, {x: "arm", y1: "Q", y2: "hi", fill: (d) => d.next ? pal.magenta : pal.blue, fillOpacity: 0.35}),
        Plot.dot(finite, {x: "arm", y: "Q", r: 5, fill: (d) => d.next ? pal.magenta : pal.blue}),
        Plot.text(data.filter((d) => d.hi === null), {x: "arm", y: 0, text: () => "untried\n(bonus ∞)", fill: pal.magenta}),
        Plot.text(data, {x: "arm", y: -3, dy: -8, text: (d) => `N = ${d.N}`, fill: pal.fg}),
        s.reveal ? Plot.tickY(data, {x: "arm", y: "q", stroke: pal.green, strokeWidth: 2.5}) : null
      ]
    }));
    const best = s.q.indexOf(Math.max(...s.q));
    root.querySelector(".rl-stats").innerHTML = s.t === 0
      ? "No pulls yet: every arm is untried, so UCB tries each once first."
      : `t = ${s.t}. Last pull: Arm ${s.last.a + 1}, reward ${s.last.R.toFixed(2)}. Next pull: <b>Arm ${next + 1}</b>.` +
        (s.reveal ? ` Best arm is Arm ${best + 1} (green ticks show q*).` : "");
  };
  root.onclick = (e) => {
    const {n, act} = e.target.dataset ?? {};
    if (n) for (let i = 0; i < +n; i++) s.step(ucbC);
    if (act === "reveal") s.reveal = !s.reveal;
    if (act === "reset") s.reset();
    if (n || act) render();
  };
  render();
  return root;
}

0.6.2 Theoretical Regret Bounds

The analysis below assumes rewards with bounded support , as in Auer et al.; the Gaussian testbed violates this, so there the bounds are a guide rather than a guarantee. By the Chernoff-Hoeffding bound, the probability that the true expectation exceeds the empirical mean by threshold decays exponentially:

Setting bounds this failure probability by ; this choice of bonus is UCB1, i.e. the selection rule above with . Lai and Robbins demonstrated that for any consistent allocation policy, the asymptotic cumulative regret is lower-bounded by (Lai and Robbins 1985):

The UCB1 algorithm of Auer et al. guarantees finite-time logarithmic regret (Auer et al. 2002):

0.7 Gradient Bandit Algorithms (§2.8)

Rather than estimating action values directly, gradient bandit algorithms maintain numerical preferences . Action probabilities are parameterised via a Gibbs / soft-max distribution:

0.7.1 Derivation via Stochastic Gradient Ascent

We seek to maximise the expected performance criterion . Taking the partial derivative with respect to preference :

Because , the gradient of this total probability mass is zero: . Consequently, an arbitrary scalar baseline independent of may be subtracted without inducing bias:

Recalling that the soft-max derivative is given by , we express the gradient as an expectation under policy :

Replacing the expectation with an instantaneous empirical sample yields the update:

where the baseline (with ), the average of the rewards before step , significantly attenuates variance. This formulation constitutes the stateless antecedent of the REINFORCE policy gradient algorithm (Williams 1992).

0.8 Associative Search / Contextual Bandits (§2.9)

When the agent observes a context vector prior to action selection, the task generalises to learning a contextual mapping . Crucially, while reward is contingent upon both state and action , action exerts no causal influence over the subsequent context . When action selection actively steers state transitions, the problem transitions formally from an associative bandit into a full Markov Decision Process.

0.9 Empirical Implementation in Python / NumPy

Below is a self-contained implementation of all four strategies on the 10-armed testbed, plus a contextual -greedy agent for §2.9. Every method records whether it chose the optimal arm at each step, so the strategies can be compared directly.

import numpy as np


class BanditTestbed:
    """k-armed Gaussian testbed (Sutton & Barto §2.3), optionally drifting (Exercise 2.5)."""

    def __init__(self, k: int = 10, stationary: bool = True, offset: float = 0.0, seed: int = 42):
        self.k = k
        self.stationary = stationary
        self.rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
        self.q_true = self.rng.normal(offset, 1.0, size=k)

    def optimal_action(self) -> int:
        return int(np.argmax(self.q_true))

    def step(self, action: int) -> float:
        reward = self.rng.normal(self.q_true[action], 1.0)
        if not self.stationary:
            self.q_true += self.rng.normal(0.0, 0.01, size=self.k)
        return float(reward)


def argmax_random(values: np.ndarray, rng: np.random.Generator) -> int:
    """Argmax with ties broken uniformly at random (avoids a systematic left-arm bias)."""
    return int(rng.choice(np.flatnonzero(values == values.max())))


def run_epsilon_greedy(env, steps=1000, epsilon=0.1, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    q_est, counts = np.zeros(env.k), np.zeros(env.k)
    optimal = np.empty(steps, dtype=bool)
    for t in range(steps):
        action = int(rng.integers(env.k)) if rng.random() < epsilon else argmax_random(q_est, rng)
        optimal[t] = action == env.optimal_action()
        r = env.step(action)
        counts[action] += 1
        q_est[action] += (r - q_est[action]) / counts[action]
    return optimal


def run_optimistic_greedy(env, steps=1000, q0=5.0, alpha=0.1, seed=0):
    # Constant step size: with 1/n the optimistic prior is erased after one pull.
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    q_est = np.full(env.k, q0)
    optimal = np.empty(steps, dtype=bool)
    for t in range(steps):
        action = argmax_random(q_est, rng)
        optimal[t] = action == env.optimal_action()
        r = env.step(action)
        q_est[action] += alpha * (r - q_est[action])
    return optimal


def run_ucb(env, steps=1000, c=2.0, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    q_est, counts = np.zeros(env.k), np.zeros(env.k)
    optimal = np.empty(steps, dtype=bool)
    for t in range(1, steps + 1):
        # Untried arms get an infinite bonus, so each is pulled once first.
        with np.errstate(divide="ignore", invalid="ignore"):
            ucb = np.where(counts == 0, np.inf, q_est + c * np.sqrt(np.log(t) / counts))
        action = argmax_random(ucb, rng)
        optimal[t - 1] = action == env.optimal_action()
        r = env.step(action)
        counts[action] += 1
        q_est[action] += (r - q_est[action]) / counts[action]
    return optimal


def run_gradient(env, steps=1000, alpha=0.1, baseline=True, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    H = np.zeros(env.k)
    mean_reward = 0.0  # average of rewards before the current step
    optimal = np.empty(steps, dtype=bool)
    for t in range(steps):
        pi = np.exp(H - H.max())
        pi /= pi.sum()
        action = int(rng.choice(env.k, p=pi))
        optimal[t] = action == env.optimal_action()
        r = env.step(action)
        b = (r if t == 0 else mean_reward) if baseline else 0.0
        one_hot = np.zeros(env.k)
        one_hot[action] = 1.0
        H += alpha * (r - b) * (one_hot - pi)
        mean_reward += (r - mean_reward) / (t + 1)
    return optimal


def run_contextual_epsilon_greedy(n_contexts=2, k=10, steps=2000, epsilon=0.1, seed=0):
    """Associative search: one action-value table per observed context (the lamp colour)."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    q_true = rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, size=(n_contexts, k))
    q_est, counts = np.zeros((n_contexts, k)), np.zeros((n_contexts, k))
    optimal = np.empty(steps, dtype=bool)
    for t in range(steps):
        x = int(rng.integers(n_contexts))  # the context does not depend on past actions
        action = int(rng.integers(k)) if rng.random() < epsilon else argmax_random(q_est[x], rng)
        optimal[t] = action == np.argmax(q_true[x])
        r = rng.normal(q_true[x, action], 1.0)
        counts[x, action] += 1
        q_est[x, action] += (r - q_est[x, action]) / counts[x, action]
    return optimal


def compare(runs=200, steps=1000):
    """Percentage of optimal actions per step, averaged over independent testbeds."""
    methods = {
        "epsilon-greedy (0.1)": run_epsilon_greedy,
        "optimistic greedy (Q1=5, alpha=0.1)": run_optimistic_greedy,
        "UCB (c=2)": run_ucb,
        "gradient (alpha=0.1, baseline)": run_gradient,
    }
    pct = {name: np.zeros(steps) for name in methods}
    for run in range(runs):
        for name, method in methods.items():
            pct[name] += method(BanditTestbed(seed=run), steps, seed=run)
    return {name: 100.0 * total / runs for name, total in pct.items()}

Running the comparison over 200 independent testbeds reproduces the ordering of Sutton & Barto’s Figures 2.3 to 2.5:

results = compare(runs=200, steps=1000)
for name, curve in results.items():
    print(f"{name:38s} last 100 steps: {curve[-100:].mean():.1f}% optimal")
ctx = run_contextual_epsilon_greedy(steps=2000)
print(f"contextual epsilon-greedy, last 500 steps: {100 * ctx[-500:].mean():.1f}% optimal")
epsilon-greedy (0.1)                   last 100 steps: 78.8% optimal
optimistic greedy (Q1=5, alpha=0.1)    last 100 steps: 85.4% optimal
UCB (c=2)                              last 100 steps: 84.6% optimal
gradient (alpha=0.1, baseline)         last 100 steps: 81.8% optimal
contextual epsilon-greedy, last 500 steps: 91.4% optimal

1 Game Theory Corner

In multi-agent settings, deterministic greedy exploration frequently fails because adversarial opponents actively exploit predictable empirical routines. When opposing payoff surfaces adapt dynamically, optimal behaviour requires mixed strategies—randomising deliberately across action spaces (as in zero-sum games such as rock-paper-scissors) to prevent an opponent from driving value updates into degenerate equilibria.

2 Key Takeaways & Glossary

Symbol / Concept Formal Definition Operational Significance
Optimistic initial estimate, Front-loads exploration; needs a constant step size to persist beyond one pull.
UCB bonus Directs exploration towards rarely tried actions; gives UCB1.
Regret of UCB1 Logarithmic, versus linear for constant -greedy.
Action preference Only differences matter; the soft-max turns preferences into probabilities.
Stochastic policy of the gradient bandit.
Mean of rewards before step Baseline that reduces gradient variance without introducing bias.
Contextual bandit Policy ; actions do not affect Bridge between bandits and full Markov Decision Processes.

3 Next in the Series

So far, actions have changed only the reward, never the situation the agent finds itself in next. In Season 1, Episode 03 (upcoming), we let actions steer the state, formalising finite Markov Decision Processes, returns, and the Bellman equations (Sutton and Barto 2018, chap. 3).

item.title: Which Candy Machine? Multi-Armed Bandits and Exploration
item.dc:creator: Varun Ravi Varma
item.description:
NoteIn brief

In the inaugural episode, we explored tic-tac-toe to examine how delayed evaluative credit propagates across sequential state transitions. Before formalising general Markov Decision Processes, we isolate the fundamental engine of reinforcement learning: evaluative feedback in a stateless setting. This episode introduces the -armed bandit problem—formalising the tension between exploiting known empirical payoff estimates and exploring uncertain alternatives, deriving incremental update rules, analysing the linear regret of -greedy selection, and establishing convergence criteria under both stationary and non-stationary distributions (Sutton and Barto 2018; Robbins and Monro 1951).

0.1 Episode Metadata

  • Game: Candy machines (-armed bandit)
  • Source: Sutton & Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (2nd ed.), Chapter 2, §2.1–2.5 (Sutton and Barto 2018)
  • Series Index: RL from First Principles
  • Story
  • Idea
  • Maths & Code

The autumn fairground is a kaleidoscope of spinning lights, whirling carousels, and cheerful music. Grandpa Leo hands Ada a little velvet pouch containing shiny metal tokens. In a sheltered wooden booth stand three gleaming vintage candy dispensers: one painted red, one blue, and one green.

“Each pull costs exactly one token,” Grandpa Leo explains, leaning against the booth counter. “Each machine drops a handful of sweets. However, their mechanisms are somewhat erratic. Sometimes a dispenser yields a generous handful; other times it dispenses merely a few.”

Ada eagerly inserts her first token into the red machine. Two strawberry drops clatter into the tray. Next, she tests the blue dispenser. A delightful burst of five lemon sweets cascades down! Finally, she tries the green machine. A solitary mint drop emerges.

“Blue is the undisputed champion!” Ada exclaims with delight. She promptly drops another token into the blue lever. Three sweets clatter out. She inserts another token. Two sweets. Another token yields only one sweet.

“Hmm,” Grandpa Leo muses, adjusting his spectacles. “Was the blue dispenser genuinely superior, or was that initial five-sweet drop merely an exceptionally fortunate fluke?”

Ada pauses and wrinkles her nose. She retrieves a small paper napkin and a stubby crayon from her coat pocket. She sketches three neat columns: one for each colour. For every machine, she totals all the sweets dispensed and divides them evenly across the tokens spent on that dispenser—calculating the fair share of sweets earned per token.

She soon notices an intriguing tension. The more tokens she expends on a machine, the more reliably she characterises its typical payout. Yet, if she continues pouring every token exclusively into the blue dispenser, she will remain completely oblivious as to whether the red or green machine harbours a superior payout in the long run.

Ada devises a methodical rule: Most of the time, she pulls whichever machine currently boasts the highest average on her napkin. However, every few turns, she deliberately pulls a different dispenser at random, purely to satisfy her curiosity.

By late afternoon, her velvet pouch is overflowing. The green dispenser—which had begun so disappointingly with a single mint—gradually revealed itself to be the most bountiful machine of all, routinely dropping four to six sweets. Ada only discovered its true nature because she refused to let early luck dictate her decisions.

TipWhat Would You Do?

If one machine awards you a massive prize on your very first turn, would you ever consider pulling an alternative machine that previously gave you almost nothing? Why?

0.2 Isolating Evaluative Feedback

In Episode 00, tic-tac-toe required solving two coupled challenges simultaneously:

  1. Evaluative Feedback: Assessing how desirable a chosen action was without an explicit supervisory gradient.
  2. Delayed Credit Assignment: Propagating scalar terminal rewards backward through a directed sequence of board configurations.

To master reinforcement learning from first principles, we temporarily step back from sequential state transitions. The multi-armed bandit framework isolates pure evaluative feedback in a single, recurring decision context.

0.3 The Fundamental Dilemma

At each round : - Exploitation: Select the action whose estimated value is currently maximal to capitalise on acquired knowledge and secure immediate reward. - Exploration: Select non-greedy actions to reduce epistemic uncertainty, refine parameter estimates, and potentially uncover vastly superior alternatives.

Crucially, an agent can never exploit and explore simultaneously with a single action. Exploiting maximises immediate expected reward on the current step; exploring sacrifices instantaneous reward to acquire information that elevates future returns.

0.4 What to Notice in the Interactive Widgets

  1. The Greed Trap (): A purely greedy agent locks irrevocably onto the first arm that produces an early positive fluctuation, often occluding the globally optimal arm forever.
  2. The Asymptotic Plateau ( vs ): A higher exploration rate () discovers the optimal arm rapidly, but plateaus below optimal performance because it continues wasting of its actions on random choices. Conversely, learns more conservatively but attains a higher asymptotic ceiling.
  3. Variance Shrinkage: As pull count grows, the empirical sample average stabilizes, corroborating the Weak Law of Large Numbers.

0.5 Try It: Ada’s Napkin

Play Ada’s afternoon yourself. Each machine drops a noisy handful of sweets around a hidden average; the napkin keeps the running average and pull count for each. Pull by hand, or let Ada’s rule (-greedy with ) choose for you, then reveal the true averages.

import {makeRng, argmaxRandom, runTestbed, toRows, observeTheme, palette} from "../../assets/ojs/rl.js"
theme = Generators.observe(observeTheme)
pal = palette(theme)
candyBooth = {
  const rng = makeRng(Date.now() >>> 0);
  // Hidden mean sweets per pull; green is best, as in the story.
  const machines = [
    {name: "Red", cls: "red", mean: 2.0},
    {name: "Blue", cls: "blue", mean: 2.6},
    {name: "Green", cls: "green", mean: 4.8}
  ];
  let N, Q, total, pulls, last, revealed;
  const root = html`<div>
    <div class="rl-widget-title">Three candy machines</div>
    <div class="rl-machines"></div>
    <div class="rl-stats"></div>
    <div>
      <button data-act="ada">Ada's rule: 1 pull</button>
      <button data-act="ada10">Ada's rule: 10 pulls</button>
      <button data-act="reveal">Reveal true averages</button>
      <button data-act="reset">Reset</button>
    </div>
    <p class="rl-note">Sweets per pull are a rounded Gaussian (sd 1.5) around each machine's hidden average.</p>
  </div>`;
  const row = root.querySelector(".rl-machines");
  const stats = root.querySelector(".rl-stats");
  const buttons = machines.map((m, a) => {
    const b = html`<button class="rl-machine ${m.cls}"></button>`;
    b.onclick = () => { pull(a); render(); };
    row.append(b);
    return b;
  });
  const reset = () => {
    N = [0, 0, 0]; Q = [0, 0, 0]; total = 0; pulls = 0; last = null; revealed = false;
  };
  const pull = (a) => {
    const sweets = Math.max(0, Math.round(rng.normal(machines[a].mean, 1.5)));
    N[a] += 1;
    Q[a] += (sweets - Q[a]) / N[a];
    total += sweets;
    pulls += 1;
    last = {a, sweets};
  };
  const adaPull = () => {
    // Untried machines first, then epsilon-greedy on the napkin averages.
    const untried = [0, 1, 2].filter((a) => N[a] === 0);
    const a = untried.length ? untried[0]
      : rng.random() < 0.1 ? rng.int(3) : argmaxRandom(Q, rng);
    pull(a);
  };
  const render = () => {
    buttons.forEach((b, a) => {
      const m = machines[a];
      b.classList.toggle("last", last !== null && last.a === a);
      b.innerHTML = `<div class="rl-machine-name">${m.name}</div>
        <div>N = ${N[a]}</div>
        <div>Q = ${N[a] ? Q[a].toFixed(2) : "–"}</div>
        ${revealed ? `<div>q* = ${m.mean.toFixed(1)}</div>` : ""}`;
    });
    stats.innerHTML = pulls === 0
      ? "Click a machine to spend a token."
      : `Pull ${pulls}: <b>${machines[last.a].name}</b> dropped ${last.sweets} sweet${last.sweets === 1 ? "" : "s"}.
         Total ${total} sweets, ${(total / pulls).toFixed(2)} per token
         (best possible on average: ${machines[2].mean.toFixed(1)}).`;
  };
  root.onclick = (e) => {
    const act = e.target.dataset?.act;
    if (!act) return;
    if (act === "ada") adaPull();
    if (act === "ada10") for (let i = 0; i < 10; i++) adaPull();
    if (act === "reveal") revealed = !revealed;
    if (act === "reset") reset();
    render();
  };
  reset();
  render();
  return root;
}

0.6 Try It: The 10-Armed Testbed

The same comparison as Sutton & Barto’s Figure 2.2, simulated live in your browser. Each curve averages many independent 10-armed problems with and rewards . Switch on drifting machines (Sutton & Barto’s Exercise 2.5: all true values start equal and take small Gaussian random-walk steps) and compare the two step-size rules: the sample average freezes, while constant keeps tracking the moving optimum.

viewof testbed = Inputs.form({
  runs: Inputs.range([50, 1000], {step: 50, value: 200, label: "Problems averaged"}),
  stepRule: Inputs.radio(["sample average (1/n)", "constant α = 0.1"], {value: "sample average (1/n)", label: "Step size"}),
  drift: Inputs.toggle({label: "Drifting machines", value: false}),
  seed: Inputs.range([1, 100], {step: 1, value: 1, label: "Seed"})
})
testbedRows = {
  const steps = testbed.drift ? 3000 : 1000;
  const alpha = testbed.stepRule.startsWith("constant") ? 0.1 : null;
  const series = [0, 0.01, 0.1].map((epsilon) => ({
    name: `ε = ${epsilon}`,
    ...runTestbed({epsilon, alpha, steps, runs: testbed.runs, seed: testbed.seed, nonstationary: testbed.drift})
  }));
  return toRows(series, steps / 200);
}
testbedPlot = (y, label, domain) => Plot.plot({
  width: Math.min(width, 760),
  height: 240,
  marginLeft: 50,
  style: {background: "transparent"},
  x: {label: "Step"},
  y: {label, grid: true, domain},
  color: {domain: ["ε = 0", "ε = 0.01", "ε = 0.1"], range: [pal.orange, pal.blue, pal.green], legend: true},
  marks: [Plot.lineY(testbedRows, {x: "step", y, stroke: "series", strokeWidth: 1.5}), Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: pal.muted})]
})
testbedPlot("reward", "Average reward", undefined)
testbedPlot("optimal", "% optimal action", [0, 100])
WarningCommon Misconception

Misconception: “The optimal decision is always to select the alternative that has delivered the highest average payoff so far.” Reality: The empirical average reflects only the history of observations obtained under an active sampling bias. An option with a modest initial sample mean might simply have suffered from unlucky stochastic variance. Without persistent exploration, empirical averages remain skewed.

0.7 Problem Formulation: The -Armed Bandit

Consider a system comprising discrete actions . At discrete time steps , the agent selects action and receives a scalar reward drawn from a stationary probability distribution :

The true value (expected payoff) of action is denoted :

The optimal action and its corresponding maximal value are defined as:

where represents the cumulative allocation count to action .

0.8 Action-Value Estimation and the Incremental Update

Let denote the agent’s internal estimate of immediately prior to round . Under the sample-average method, is computed as the arithmetic mean of all rewards accumulated from arm :

Computing this summation naively would require unbounded memory . Instead, we derive the classic incremental update. Consider a single action arm that has been selected times, yielding observed rewards . Upon receiving the -th reward :

This derivation exemplifies the quintessential operational paradigm across reinforcement learning:

where formalises the prediction error.

0.9 Action Selection Mechanisms

  1. Greedy Selection: Ties must be broken uniformly at random to prevent systematic left-arm bias.

  2. -Greedy Selection: With probability , select a greedy action. With probability , sample an action uniformly at random from :

As , every arm is sampled infinitely often (), guaranteeing by the Strong Law of Large Numbers. However, because a constant fraction of all pulls remains uniformly exploratory, the cumulative regret scales linearly:

0.10 Tracking Non-Stationary Environments

When reward distributions drift over time, earlier observations become progressively misleading. We replace the sample-average step size with a constant learning rate :

Expanding this recursion backwards reveals an exponential recency-weighted average:

The weight allocated to reward decays geometrically with temporal recency . Notice that the total weight distribution sums to unity:

0.11 Robbins-Monro Convergence Criteria

Under what conditions does a generic sequence of step-size parameters guarantee almost sure convergence ? The stochastic approximation theory established by Robbins & Monro (Robbins and Monro 1951) dictates two mandatory conditions:

  1. Condition 1 (): The step sizes must be sufficiently large to overcome any initial conditions or early stochastic fluctuations.
  2. Condition 2 (): The step sizes must attenuate fast enough to extinguish residual variance and guarantee convergence to a stationary point.
  • Sample Mean (): (harmonic series diverges) and . Both conditions are fulfilled; estimates converge asymptotically.
  • Constant Step-Size (): , but . The second condition fails; estimates maintain persistent responsiveness to track non-stationary changes.

0.12 Vectorised NumPy Implementation

Below is a complete, vectorised Python implementation reproducing Sutton & Barto’s 10-armed bandit testbed (§2.3) with rigorous random tie-breaking.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def run_bandit_experiment(
    n_arms: int = 10,
    n_steps: int = 1000,
    n_runs: int = 2000,
    epsilons: list[float] = [0.0, 0.01, 0.1],
    alpha: float | None = None
) -> tuple[dict[float, np.ndarray], dict[float, np.ndarray]]:
    """
    Vectorised simulation of the k-armed bandit testbed across multiple runs.
    """
    results_reward = {}
    results_optimal = {}

    for eps in epsilons:
        # Initialise true values: q_*(a) ~ N(0, 1) per run
        q_true = np.random.normal(0.0, 1.0, size=(n_runs, n_arms))
        optimal_arms = np.argmax(q_true, axis=1)

        # Value estimates Q and pull counts N
        Q = np.zeros((n_runs, n_arms))
        N = np.zeros((n_runs, n_arms), dtype=int)

        rewards_history = np.zeros((n_runs, n_steps))
        optimal_action_history = np.zeros((n_runs, n_steps))

        for t in range(n_steps):
            # Epsilon-greedy action selection
            explore_mask = np.random.uniform(0.0, 1.0, size=n_runs) < eps
            random_actions = np.random.randint(0, n_arms, size=n_runs)

            # Greedy actions with uniform random tie-breaking
            # Adding infinitesimal jitter guarantees unbiased tie-breaking
            jitter = np.random.uniform(0.0, 1e-9, size=Q.shape)
            greedy_actions = np.argmax(Q + jitter, axis=1)

            actions = np.where(explore_mask, random_actions, greedy_actions)

            # Sample observed scalar reward: R ~ N(q_*(A), 1.0)
            run_indices = np.arange(n_runs)
            rewards = np.random.normal(q_true[run_indices, actions], 1.0)

            # Update pull counts
            N[run_indices, actions] += 1

            # Update action-value estimates
            if alpha is None:
                step_sizes = 1.0 / N[run_indices, actions]
            else:
                step_sizes = alpha

            Q[run_indices, actions] += step_sizes * (rewards - Q[run_indices, actions])

            # Record metrics
            rewards_history[:, t] = rewards
            optimal_action_history[:, t] = (actions == optimal_arms)

        results_reward[eps] = np.mean(rewards_history, axis=0)
        results_optimal[eps] = np.mean(optimal_action_history, axis=0) * 100.0

    return results_reward, results_optimal
NoteGame Theory Corner

In a stationary multi-armed bandit, the environment is passive: pulling an arm does not alter its underlying reward distribution. What happens, however, when the candy machine actively observes your choices and redistributes its payouts to minimise your score? This competitive dynamic transforms the bandit into a zero-sum matrix game (e.g. matching pennies or rock-paper-scissors), where deterministic pure strategies are perpetually exploitable and optimal play necessitates randomised mixed strategies. We will explore this formal transition in our parallel game theory series.

0.13 Key Takeaways & Glossary

Symbol / Concept Formal Definition Operational Significance
Ground-truth expected return of action .
Current empirical action-value estimate prior to round .
Total allocation count to action up to time .
Suboptimality gap between optimal arm and action .
Cumulative expected regret after decision steps.
Robbins-Monro , Necessary & sufficient criteria for almost-sure parameter convergence.

0.14 What Comes Next?

While -greedy action selection guarantees asymptotic exploration, its randomised choices are indiscriminate: it explores promising and dismal alternatives with equal likelihood. In Season 1, Episode 02: Curious, but Clever, we formulate guided, directed exploration mechanisms: - Optimism in the Face of Uncertainty: Initial value biases that encourage transient, self-terminating exploration. - Upper Confidence Bound (UCB): Quantifying epistemic uncertainty via concentration bounds to attain logarithmic regret . - Gradient Bandits: Learning continuous action preference probabilities through softmax stochastic gradient ascent.

References

Robbins, Herbert, and Sutton Monro. 1951. “A Stochastic Approximation Method.” The Annals of Mathematical Statistics 22 (3): 400–407. https://doi.org/10.1214/aoms/1177729586.
Sutton, Richard S., and Andrew G. Barto. 2018. Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction. 2nd ed. MIT Press. http://incompleteideas.net/book/the-book-2nd.html.

item.title: Learning from Rewards: Tic-Tac-Toe and Value Functions
item.dc:creator: Varun Ravi Varma
item.description:
NoteIn brief

Unlike supervised learning, which relies on instructional corrective feedback from an external oracle, reinforcement learning systems discover optimal decision policies purely through active interaction, trial, error, and evaluative reward. This inaugural episode introduces the foundations of tabular value learning using the classic game of noughts and crosses (tic-tac-toe): formalising how delayed temporal credit cascades backwards through state-value estimates and how exploration mitigates sub-optimal policy collapse.

0.1 Episode Metadata

  • Game: Tic-tac-toe (Noughts and Crosses)
  • Source: Sutton & Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (2nd ed.), Chapter 1, §1.1–1.7 (Sutton and Barto 2018)
  • Series Index: RL from First Principles
  • Story
  • Idea
  • Maths & Code

Rain taps against the kitchen windowpane. Ada is six years old, and she is thoroughly bored. Grandpa Leo sets down his mug of Earl Grey tea, picks up an ink pen, and draws a crisp grid of nine squares on a sheet of scrap paper. Biscuit, his scruffy terrier, curls up quietly beneath the wooden table.

“A game of noughts and crosses,” Grandpa Leo announces with a twinkle in his eye. “You shall play crosses. I shall play noughts.”

Ada grips her pencil tightly. “How do I win, Grandpa?”

Grandpa Leo leans back in his wicker chair and smiles. “I am not going to give you instructions or tell you where to move. We shall simply play, and you will discover it yourself.”

Ada loses her very first game within four turns. She loses the second game as well. In the third encounter, however, she places her cross squarely in the centre square almost by accident. Suddenly Grandpa Leo pauses, studies the board carefully, and scratches his chin. Two moves later, Ada completes a diagonal line of three crosses. She leaps up from her chair and cheers!

Ada runs over to the dresser, grabs a small blue notebook, and flips to a clean page. Every time a match concludes, she retraces the sequence of boards that unfolded along the way. Whenever a board layout leads directly to victory, she sketches a beaming happy face beside it. Whenever a layout leads to defeat, she sketches a frown. When a match ends in a stalemate, she sketches a neutral, flat line.

After forty games across the afternoon, something magical begins to happen. Before placing her pencil onto paper, Ada glances across the empty squares and can almost feel which moves lead toward winning positions. She naturally selects the move that transitions the board into one carrying a happy face.

Occasionally, however, she deliberately tests an unusual move that she has never tried before. “Why did you place your cross in that odd corner, Ada?” laughs Grandpa Leo. “That seems like an eccentric move!”

“I am exploring,” Ada replies proudly. “Perhaps that square is secretly wonderful!”

Most of the time, the eccentric move leads nowhere special. Yet once in a while, it reveals an ingenious trap that Grandpa Leo cannot block, earning a fresh smiley face in her little notebook.

By teatime, Ada and Grandpa draw every single contest. Nobody ever handed Ada a handbook or dictated a fixed set of rules. She acquired mastery purely through interaction, rewards, and keen observation.

TipWhat Would You Do?

If nobody ever explains the optimal strategy to you, how can you still systematically improve your skill at a game?

0.2 Learning from Evaluative Feedback

The fundamental distinction separating reinforcement learning from classical supervised learning lies in the nature of feedback:

  1. Supervised Learning (Instructional Feedback): An external oracle provides ground-truth supervisory labels delineating the exact corrective action required in each scenario.
  2. Reinforcement Learning (Evaluative Feedback): The environment supplies a scalar numerical reward evaluating how favourable the outcome was, without ever indicating whether an alternative, untaken action was superior.

0.3 Why Supervision Fails Where Reinforcement Succeeds

Why can we not simply formulate game-playing and sequential control as standard supervised classification? Supervised learning requires an exhaustive training corpus of state-action pairs labelled with optimal decisions. In sequential domains, this paradigm suffers from three critical failure modes:

  1. The Oracle Paradox: For complex sequential decision problems, no omniscient human or computational oracle exists to provide optimal labels across the combinatorial explosion of states. If an expert already possessed the optimal policy for every board state, programming the system directly would be trivial, obviating the need for machine learning.
  2. Imitation Ceiling and Sub-optimal Demonstration: A supervised model trained on behavioural cloning can never surpass the skill of the teacher who supplied the training data. If Grandpa Leo plays with systematic flaws or cognitive blind spots, a supervised network dutifully replicates those blunders. Reinforcement learning, conversely, circumvents teacher bias: by learning directly from outcomes ( for win, for loss), an agent discovers creative strategies unthought of by its creators.
  3. Distributional Covariate Shift (Compounding Errors): In supervised learning, training assumes independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) data. In sequential interaction, however, an agent’s current action dictates the subsequent state distribution. If a supervised agent makes a minor prediction error, it lands in an unfamiliar state outside its training distribution. Without training data in that region, errors compound rapidly along the trajectory, leading to catastrophic failure. Reinforcement learning is inherently active and closed-loop: the agent experiences the causal consequences of its own mistakes, learning corrective recoveries directly from the environment.

0.4 Credit Assignment and Value Propagation

When playing a game, reward signals are typically delayed until termination. How does an agent determine which early opening move was genuinely responsible for a victory attained twenty turns later? This challenge is formalised as the temporal credit assignment problem.

In our tabular formulation, the agent maintains an internal lookup table assigning an estimated value to each board state , representing the long-term probability of victory from that state. Learning operates via backward propagation:

  • States containing three crosses in a row are terminal winning states: .
  • States containing three noughts in a row are terminal losing states: .
  • Stalemate boards have terminal value .
  • All intermediate states are initialised optimistically to .

As games unfold, probability values gradually cascade backwards from terminal outcomes into earlier configurations:

where denotes the step-size learning rate.

0.5 The Exploration-Exploitation Dilemma

At every decision point, an agent confronts a core trade-off:

  • Exploitation: Select the move leading to the state with the highest existing estimated value to maximise current win rate.
  • Exploration: Select an alternative move at random with probability to sample uncharted state trajectories and refine inaccurate estimates.

If an agent acts purely greedily (), it risks latching onto a sub-optimal heuristic formed through early stochastic luck. Conversely, if an agent explores excessively, it sacrifices performance by repeatedly committing catastrophic blunders.

WarningCommon Misconception

Misconception: “Reinforcement learning is merely unstructured trial and error at random.” Reality: While random sampling initiates exploration, the errors are systematically captured by the value function. Subsequent decisions are biased toward high-value basins, converting random variance into guided, goal-directed improvement.

0.6 Try It: Train Ada in Your Browser

The agent below plays crosses (moving first) against a uniformly random opponent and learns with the temporal-difference rule above, skipping updates after exploratory moves. Values are kept for afterstates, the boards right after the agent moves, as in Sutton & Barto §1.5. Change and and watch the outcome rates shift.

import {trainTicTacToe, moveValues, greedyMove, winner, LINES, rolling, makeRng, observeTheme, palette} from "../../assets/ojs/rl.js"
theme = Generators.observe(observeTheme)
pal = palette(theme)
viewof ttt = Inputs.form({
  episodes: Inputs.range([500, 20000], {step: 500, value: 5000, label: "Games"}),
  alpha: Inputs.range([0.01, 1], {step: 0.01, value: 0.1, label: "α (step size)"}),
  epsilon: Inputs.range([0, 0.5], {step: 0.01, value: 0.1, label: "ε (exploration)"}),
  seed: Inputs.range([1, 100], {step: 1, value: 42, label: "Seed"})
})
tttAgent = trainTicTacToe(ttt)
tttRows = {
  const window = 250;
  const h = tttAgent.history;
  const rows = [];
  for (const [name, v] of [["Win", 1], ["Draw", 0], ["Loss", -1]]) {
    const rate = rolling(Array.from(h, (x) => (x === v ? 100 : 0)), window);
    for (let i = window - 1; i < h.length; i += 10) rows.push({outcome: name, game: i + 1, rate: rate[i]});
  }
  return rows;
}
Plot.plot({
  width: Math.min(width, 760),
  height: 250,
  marginLeft: 45,
  style: {background: "transparent"},
  x: {label: "Game"},
  y: {label: "% of last 250 games", grid: true, domain: [0, 100]},
  color: {domain: ["Win", "Draw", "Loss"], range: [pal.green, pal.blue, pal.red], legend: true},
  marks: [Plot.lineY(tttRows, {x: "game", y: "rate", stroke: "outcome", strokeWidth: 1.5})]
})
{
  const last = tttAgent.history.slice(-1000);
  const pct = (v) => (100 * last.filter((x) => x === v).length / last.length).toFixed(1);
  return html`<p class="rl-stats">Last ${last.length} training games: win ${pct(1)}%, draw ${pct(0)}%, loss ${pct(-1)}%.
    ${tttAgent.values.size} afterstates visited.</p>
    <p class="rl-note">Losses never vanish entirely while ε > 0: the agent keeps making deliberate random moves during training.</p>`;
}

0.7 Try It: Play Against the Trained Agent

Now play noughts yourself against the agent trained above (it plays greedily here, with no exploration). Before each of its moves, the agent’s estimate of every candidate square is shown in that square’s corner. An agent trained only against a random opponent may still have blind spots against deliberate play: can you find one?

tttPlay = {
  const values = tttAgent.values;
  const rng = makeRng(Date.now() >>> 0);
  let board, status, shown, lastCell;
  const root = html`<div>
    <div class="rl-board"></div>
    <div class="rl-stats"></div>
    <div><button data-act="new">New game</button></div>
  </div>`;
  const grid = root.querySelector(".rl-board");
  const cells = Array.from({length: 9}, (_, i) => {
    const b = html`<button aria-label="Square ${i + 1}"></button>`;
    b.onclick = () => humanMove(i);
    grid.append(b);
    return b;
  });
  const winLine = () => LINES.find(([a, b, c]) => board[a] !== 0 && board[a] === board[b] && board[a] === board[c]) ?? [];
  const finish = (w) => {
    status = w === 1 ? "Agent wins." : w === -1 ? "You win! You found a hole in its value table." : "Draw.";
  };
  const agentMove = () => {
    shown = new Map(moveValues(values, board).map((m) => [m.cell, m.value]));
    lastCell = greedyMove(values, board, rng);
    board[lastCell] = 1;
    const w = winner(board);
    if (w !== null) finish(w); else status = "Your move (O).";
  };
  const humanMove = (i) => {
    if (board[i] !== 0 || winner(board) !== null) return;
    board[i] = -1;
    const w = winner(board);
    if (w !== null) { finish(w); shown = new Map(); } else agentMove();
    render();
  };
  const render = () => {
    const line = winLine();
    cells.forEach((b, i) => {
      const v = board[i];
      b.className = v === 1 ? "x" : v === -1 ? "o" : "";
      if (line.includes(i)) b.classList.add("win");
      const est = v === 0 || i === lastCell ? shown.get(i) : undefined;
      b.innerHTML = (v === 1 ? "X" : v === -1 ? "O" : "") +
        (est !== undefined ? `<span class="rl-v">${est.toFixed(2)}</span>` : "");
      b.disabled = v !== 0 || winner(board) !== null;
    });
    root.querySelector(".rl-stats").textContent = status;
  };
  const newGame = () => {
    board = new Array(9).fill(0);
    agentMove();
    render();
  };
  root.querySelector("[data-act=new]").onclick = newGame;
  newGame();
  return root;
}

Corner numbers are the values the agent saw for each square just before its last move, including the square it chose.

0.8 Mathematical Formalisation

0.8.1 Foundational Elements of Reinforcement Learning

Following Sutton and Barto (2018, sec. 1.3), a reinforcement learning system is characterised by four integral sub-elements:

  1. Policy (): A mapping , where delineates the agent’s behavioural disposition across valid actions.
  2. Reward Signal (): An immediate scalar evaluative feedback transmitted by the environment at each discrete transition, defining the operational objective.
  3. Value Function ( vs ): Whereas reward specifies immediate desirability, the state-value function quantifies the expected cumulative return over the long-term horizon, taking into account the states likely to follow.
  4. Model of the Environment: An internal representation of transition dynamics. In tic-tac-toe, the agent leverages a simple 1-step lookahead model of the game rules to evaluate candidate moves directly via state values , circumventing the requirement for model-free action-value functions .

0.8.2 The Markov Decision Process Formalism

We model the learning agent under the formalism of a discrete-time Markov Decision Process (MDP) defined by the 5-tuple :

  • State Space (): The finite set of valid 9-cell board configurations, with representing the board state at turn .
  • Action Space (): The state-dependent set of legal placements available in unoccupied squares.
  • Transition Dynamics (): The transition probability kernel . In a two-player game, a single environment transition folds the agent’s placement together with the opponent’s subsequent counter-action , preserving the Markov property from the agent’s perspective against a stationary opponent.
  • Reward Function (): Immediate scalar feedback . Intermediate step rewards are zero, with evaluative payoffs allocated at episode termination :
  • Discount Factor (): The parameter weighting future vs immediate returns. Because tic-tac-toe is an episodic game with guaranteed finite termination (), we set (undiscounted episodic return).

0.8.3 Trajectory, Return, and State Value

An episode generates a finite trajectory . The return denotes the cumulative discounted reward accumulated from time step :

With and zero intermediate rewards, . The state-value function under policy represents the expected return contingent upon starting from state :

0.8.4 Why Supervised Loss Fails: Empirical Risk vs Bellman Consistency

In supervised learning, an agent minimises empirical cross-entropy loss over a static dataset of teacher transitions :

This objective treats transitions as independent and identically distributed. Under sequential rollouts, however, policy deviations induce covariate shift: the true visitation distribution diverges from the demonstration distribution , causing error growth proportional to over horizon (the compounding error bound of behavioural cloning).

Reinforcement learning replaces empirical label fitting with Bellman consistency. Rather than matching arbitrary teacher actions, the objective aligns state evaluations with realized environmental returns:

Because the state distribution is generated by the agent’s own interaction, any trajectory diversion automatically populates the value table with corrective feedback, ensuring stability and surpassing human demonstration bounds.

0.8.5 The Temporal-Difference Update Rule

Here denotes the afterstate, the board immediately after the agent’s move at turn , so the transition spans the opponent’s counter-move and the agent’s next move. Following each non-exploratory transition, the value estimate is updated via:

where:

  • is the current value estimate of state .
  • serves as the bootstrapping target—the foundational principle of updating an existing evaluation estimate from subsequent estimates rather than awaiting the empirical terminal return at episode conclusion.
  • is the temporal-difference (TD) error (recalling for non-terminal transitions and ).
  • is the step-size parameter governing the learning rate.

If is reduced gradually satisfying the Robbins-Monro conditions and , converges asymptotically to the true win probabilities against any stationary opponent (Sutton and Barto 2018).

ImportantWhy Are Exploratory Moves Excluded from Updates?

In the classic formulation of Sutton and Barto §1.5, when the agent takes an exploratory move, the prior state is not updated using the value of the exploratory successor. Learning from exploratory actions would bias the value function toward reflecting the consequences of irrational exploratory blunders rather than the value of states under greedy execution. This serves as an early pedagogical precursor to off-policy Q-learning (Watkins and Dayan 1992).

0.9 Algorithmic Specification

Algorithm: Tabular TD(0) Value Learning for Tic-Tac-Toe
Initialize V(s) = 0.5 for all non-terminal states s in S
Initialize V(s) = 1.0 for winning terminal states
Initialize V(s) = 0.0 for losing terminal states
Initialize V(s) = 0.5 for draw terminal states

V is indexed by afterstates: boards immediately after the agent has moved.

For each training episode:
    board = Initial empty board
    prev = None                      # last greedy afterstate awaiting its target
    Loop:
        With probability epsilon:
            a = UniformRandomChoice(legal_actions(board))
            exploratory = True
        Else:
            a = argmax_{a' in legal_actions(board)} V(successor(board, a'))
            exploratory = False

        after = successor(board, a)
        If prev is not None and not exploratory:
            V(prev) <- V(prev) + alpha * [V(after) - V(prev)]
        prev = None if exploratory else after
        If after is terminal: stop

        Opponent chooses move a_opp
        board = successor(after, a_opp)
        If board is terminal:
            If prev is not None:
                V(prev) <- V(prev) + alpha * [V_terminal(board) - V(prev)]
            stop

0.10 Complete NumPy Implementation

Below is a self-contained, reproducible Python implementation of the tabular value iteration agent playing against both random and heuristic opponents:

import numpy as np

class TicTacToe:
    def __init__(self):
        self.board = np.zeros(9, dtype=int)
        
    def reset(self):
        self.board.fill(0)
        return self.get_state()

    def get_state(self):
        return tuple(self.board)

    def legal_moves(self):
        return np.where(self.board == 0)[0]

    def make_move(self, action, player):
        self.board[action] = player

    def check_winner(self):
        wins = [
            (0, 1, 2), (3, 4, 5), (6, 7, 8),
            (0, 3, 6), (1, 4, 7), (2, 5, 8),
            (0, 4, 8), (2, 4, 6)
        ]
        for a, b, c in wins:
            if self.board[a] != 0 and self.board[a] == self.board[b] == self.board[c]:
                return self.board[a]
        if len(self.legal_moves()) == 0:
            return 0  # Draw
        return None  # Ongoing


class TabularRLAgent:
    def __init__(self, alpha=0.1, epsilon=0.1, seed=42):
        self.alpha = alpha
        self.epsilon = epsilon
        self.values = {}
        self.rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)

    def get_value(self, state, winner=None):
        if winner == 1:
            return 1.0
        elif winner == -1:
            return 0.0
        elif winner == 0:
            return 0.5
        return self.values.get(state, 0.5)

    def select_action(self, env, explore=True):
        moves = env.legal_moves()
        if explore and self.rng.random() < self.epsilon:
            return self.rng.choice(moves), True

        best_val = -np.inf
        best_moves = []
        for m in moves:
            env.make_move(m, 1)
            winner = env.check_winner()
            val = self.get_value(env.get_state(), winner)
            env.make_move(m, 0)

            if val > best_val:
                best_val = val
                best_moves = [m]
            elif np.isclose(val, best_val):
                best_moves.append(m)

        action = self.rng.choice(best_moves)
        return action, False

    def update(self, afterstate, target):
        v = self.get_value(afterstate)
        self.values[afterstate] = v + self.alpha * (target - v)


def train(episodes=10_000, alpha=0.1, epsilon=0.1, seed=42):
    agent = TabularRLAgent(alpha=alpha, epsilon=epsilon, seed=seed)
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    history = []

    for ep in range(episodes):
        env = TicTacToe()
        env.reset()
        prev = None  # last greedy afterstate, waiting for its TD target

        while True:
            action, explored = agent.select_action(env, explore=True)
            env.make_move(action, 1)
            winner = env.check_winner()
            after = env.get_state()

            # TD(0) between consecutive afterstates; skip exploratory moves.
            if prev is not None and not explored:
                agent.update(prev, agent.get_value(after, winner))
            prev = None if explored else after

            if winner is not None:
                history.append(winner)
                break

            # Opponent turn: Random policy
            opp_action = rng.choice(env.legal_moves())
            env.make_move(opp_action, -1)
            winner = env.check_winner()

            if winner is not None:
                # Back the final outcome up into our last afterstate.
                if prev is not None:
                    agent.update(prev, agent.get_value(None, winner))
                history.append(winner)
                break

    return agent, np.array(history)

0.11 Empirical Evaluation

Against a random opponent the agent wins most games from the start, and training mainly removes its remaining losses. With and (seed 42), the loss rate falls from 3.9% in the first 1,000 games to 1.0% in the last 1,000, while the win rate rises from 93.0% to 96.1%. Losses never reach zero during training: with the agent keeps making deliberate random moves, some of which hand the opponent a win. (The browser widget in the Idea tab uses a different random number generator, so its exact figures differ.)

agent, hist = train(episodes=10_000, alpha=0.1, epsilon=0.1)

# Windowed win-rate calculation
window = 500
wins = np.convolve(hist == 1, np.ones(window)/window, mode='valid')
draws = np.convolve(hist == 0, np.ones(window)/window, mode='valid')
losses = np.convolve(hist == -1, np.ones(window)/window, mode='valid')

print(f"Final 1,000 Games Performance:")
print(f"  Win Rate:  {np.mean(hist[-1000:] == 1) * 100:.1f}%")
print(f"  Draw Rate: {np.mean(hist[-1000:] == 0) * 100:.1f}%")
print(f"  Loss Rate: {np.mean(hist[-1000:] == -1) * 100:.1f}%")

1 Game Theory Corner

From an game-theoretic standpoint, tic-tac-toe is a finite, extensive-form, two-player zero-sum game with perfect information (Neumann and Morgenstern 1944). By Zermelo’s theorem, there exists a unique game-theoretic value under backwards induction: with optimal backward play, the game is a deterministic draw.

Arthur Samuel’s seminal 1959 checkers player (Samuel 1959) demonstrated that learning state values via linear parameter updates can approximate minimax tree search without exhaustive combinatorial expansion. When our tabular agent plays against an unvarying suboptimal adversary, it does not seek the game-theoretic minimax equilibrium; rather, it actively exploits the opponent’s systematic idiosyncrasies to maximise empirical payoff.

2 Glossary

  • Agent: The active entity that observes state, computes policy, and executes actions.
  • Environment: Everything external to the agent, specifying the transition dynamics and reward responses.
  • State (): The complete informational representation of the current configuration.
  • Value Function (): The expected cumulative discounted future reward conditional on starting in state .
  • Temporal-Difference Error (): The discrepancy between successive state value estimates: .
  • Exploration vs Exploitation: The essential trade-off between trying novel actions to acquire information versus choosing known high-reward actions.
